traveler: José Antonio de Aguirre y Lecube
title: The Oath Under the Tree: the First Lehendakari, the False Panamanian, and Twenty-One Years of a Government Without a Country
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Chocolate House and the Ikastola

stops.name: Bilbao, the birth on Calle de la Cruz
stops.date_confidence: attested for date and city (euskadi.eus, Basque Government lehendakari biography, 6 March 1904, Bilbao); the street address, 6 Calle de la Cruz, and the same-day baptism come from the background dossier alone and are not confirmed by any source fetched. Flagged contradiction: one Wikipedia summary fetch rendered the birth as 1 March 1904 against euskadi.eus's 6 March; not resolved here.
stops.campa: A son is born to Teodoro de Aguirre and Bernardina Lecube in a house in the old quarter of Bilbao, and is baptized the same day. The family trade is chocolate, the ordinary prosperous trade of a Basque bourgeois household that speaks Basque at home and Spanish across the counter. The date is 6 March 1904 by the Basque Government's own reckoning; one summary of his life puts the birth five days earlier, on the first of the month, and the two have never been reconciled. Outside, Bilbao is ore barges, blast furnaces, and a river running the colour of the foundries that line it.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque marking Aguirre's birthplace in Bilbao's Casco Viejo

stops.name: Bilbao, the ikastola under the arcades
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. English Wikipedia states only that he attended 'the Basque Country's first Ikastola' and names no location; the Plaza Nueva siting and the age range come from background material and were not confirmed by any source fetched. Date set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He is sent to a school where the lessons are given in Basque, remembered afterward as among the first ikastolas in the country. The language has no official standing, no state grammar, no ministry, no examinations; it survives in kitchens, on fishing boats, and in a handful of rooms like this one. Which room is no longer certain. The tradition puts it under the arcades of the Plaza Nueva, which enclose a square of stone where the children are let out to run. A school has been built around the language, and he is six years old inside it.
suggested_refs: The Plaza Nueva arcades, Bilbao Casco Viejo

stops.name: Orduña, the Jesuit boarders' school
stops.date_confidence: attested that he began secondary schooling with the Jesuits at Orduña (Basque Wikipedia: 'Bigarren Hezkuntzako ikasketak Urduñako jesuiten ikastetxean hasi zituen'); the school is named as the Colegio de Santa María de la Antigua by cuadernosdefutbol.com. The year is set to order the segment. Coordinates are the Orduña town centre, corrected from a dossier value that fell about 5 km outside the municipality.
stops.campa: Secondary schooling begins at the Colegio de Santa María de la Antigua, the Jesuit house at Orduña in the Biscayan uplands, an hour and a world away from the estuary. The regime is boarding-school Catholicism: Latin, rhetoric, examinations of conscience, a bell for every hour of the day. He is a good student and a better athlete. What the Jesuits give him is the vocabulary he will use for the rest of his political life, Christian first and nationalist second, and he never afterwards pretends the order runs the other way. He is twelve years old when he arrives.
suggested_refs: The Colegio de Santa María de la Antigua, Orduña, Jesuit secondary school
sources: cuadernosdefutbol.com (CIHEFE), 'José Antonio Aguirre Lecube: el fútbol una afición, la política una pasión'

stops.name: Algorta, the father's death
stops.date_confidence: attested (English Wikipedia): Teodoro de Aguirre dies in 1920, the family moves to Algorta in Getxo, and the sixteen-year-old becomes head of household and of the family chocolate business. The specific house has not been located; the coordinate is town level.
stops.campa: Teodoro dies and the household shifts across to Algorta, in Getxo, on the seaward side of the estuary. José Antonio is sixteen. He takes on the chocolate firm, the accounts, his mother, his sisters. A sixteen-year-old signing for a firm has to hold a room of older men or lose the firm, and he holds the room. He also goes on playing football and goes on reading for a law degree. For five years the three run in parallel, and no source says which of them he took to be the main one.
suggested_refs: The Aguirre family chocolate firm of Bilbao

stops.name: Bilbao, San Mamés: the debut
stops.date_confidence: attested for the debut (cuadernosdefutbol.com: 27 November 1921 against S.D. Deusto in the Campeonato Regional del Norte). The appearance and goal counts are disputed across sources: Basque Wikipedia gives 46 matches, cuadernosdefutbol 'una cincuentena' including friendlies plus four goals in three regional matches in 1924-25, and the career is bracketed 1921-1925 by English and Spanish Wikipedia against 1921-22 to 1925-26 by cuadernosdefutbol. Coordinates are the old San Mamés, corrected from a dossier latitude about 370 m off.
stops.campa: He debuts for Athletic Club on 27 November 1921 against S.D. Deusto in the Campeonato Regional del Norte, inside forward, seventeen years old. He is a squad player rather than a fixture, and the record of what he actually did is not agreed: forty-six matches by one count, close to fifty including friendlies by another, four goals in three regional matches in the season of 1924-25. San Mamés is already the loudest room in Bizkaia. On 2 March 1924 he plays a friendly at Las Llanas de Sestao against Sestao Sport, and it finishes nil-nil.
suggested_refs: Athletic Club historical squad records, 1921-22 to 1925-26
The demolished old San Mamés stadium, closed 2013

stops.name: Bilbao, Deusto: the licenciatura
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by cuadernosdefutbol.com ('obtuvo el título de Licenciado el 23 de noviembre de 1925'), which resolves in favour of 1925 a contradiction between the background dossier (1925) and both English Wikipedia and sabinoarana.eus (1926). The office address is itself contested: the dossier gives Calle Iturribide 2, cuadernosdefutbol says opposite the Calzadas de Mallona. Deusto coordinates corrected from a dossier value about 1.3 km off campus.
stops.campa: He takes his licenciatura in law from the Jesuit University of Deusto on 23 November 1925, at twenty-one, having read for it while running a chocolate firm and playing first-team football. One specialist account gives the day; two others put the degree a year later, and the disagreement has never been settled. He opens his own office in the Casco Viejo, opposite the Calzadas de Mallona, the long stair that climbs to the cemetery. A young lawyer in Bilbao in the late twenties handles leases, wills, and the quarrels of a city swelling on iron money.
suggested_refs: The Calzadas de Mallona, Bilbao Casco Viejo, site of his law office
sources: sabinoarana.eus, 'Un mito llamado José Antonio Agirre'

stops.name: Getxo, the youngest mayor
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was elected councillor in the municipal elections of April 1931 and became mayor of Getxo at twenty-seven (Spanish and English Wikipedia). The town hall building itself is a reasonable reconstruction of the coordinate, not independently verified.
stops.campa: The municipal elections of 12 April 1931 bring down a monarchy. The day after, he is a councillor in Getxo, and shortly afterward its mayor, twenty-seven years old. The Republic is four days old and the Basque mayors are already organizing. He becomes their visible convener, a young man in a good suit who can hold a room of alcaldes from three provinces and get them to put their names to the same document. The office is a small one. He resigns it inside fifteen months for a seat in Madrid.
suggested_refs: The assembly movement of Basque mayors for autonomy, 1931

stops.name: Estella, the statute of the four provinces
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Estella Statute project of 1931 is widely reported, but no source fetched in this pass names Estella in connection with Aguirre personally; the coordinate is the town centre and the day is set to order the segment. Flagged as a gap rather than dropped.
stops.campa: At Estella the mayors put their names to a statute for four provinces, Alava, Gipuzkoa, Bizkaia and Navarre together, drafted alongside Carlist allies who share his Catholicism and nothing else whatever. He argues for the text in the terms he will use for the next thirty years: that a nation with its own language and its own body of law is entitled to govern itself, and that this is not a favour in anybody's gift. Madrid will not take it. Navarre will fall away. The Carlists signing beside him in 1931 will be shooting at his government by 1936.
suggested_refs: The Estella Statute project of 1931, for Alava, Gipuzkoa, Bizkaia and Navarre

stops.name: Madrid, the Constituent Cortes
stops.date_confidence: attested (Spanish Wikipedia): elected deputy to the Constituent Cortes for Navarre on 12 July 1931 on the pro-statute Catholic-nationalist coalition ticket, resigning the Getxo mayoralty to concentrate on parliamentary work. The chamber is the standard seat of the Cortes; his personal attendance at that building is not separately documented.
stops.campa: Elected on 12 July 1931 to the Constituent Cortes for Navarre, on a Catholic-nationalist ticket built around the statute, he gives up Getxo and moves into the chamber on the Carrera de San Jerónimo. He is twenty-seven, and his entire mandate is a single question. Republican Spain cannot place him: too Catholic for the left, too Basque for the right. He will not trade the statute to either side in exchange for protection, and for five years that is the whole of his parliamentary position.
suggested_refs: The Congreso de los Diputados, Carrera de San Jerónimo, Madrid

stops.name: Bilbao, Begoña: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested by Basque Wikipedia, verbatim: '1933ko irailaren 8an, Bilboko Begoñako basilikan Mari Carmen Zabalarekin ezkondu zen', giving 8 September 1933 at the Basilica of Begoña and a daughter, Aintzane. This corrects the background dossier, which gave 8 July 1933 and no church.
stops.campa: On 8 September 1933 he marries María del Carmen Zabala in the Basilica of Begoña, above Bilbao, the sanctuary the whole city climbs to. A daughter, Aintzane, follows. He is twenty-nine and has been a deputy for two years, and he marries at home, in the church that stands over the city he represents from Madrid. Begoña is the ordinary church of ordinary Bilbao weddings, and it is also the hill from which the entire industrial estuary can be seen at once, the cranes and the ore quays and the smoke.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of Begoña, Bilbao

stops.name: Bilbao, the referendum of the three provinces
stops.date_confidence: attested (Spanish Wikipedia) for the referendum of 5 November 1933 in Alava, Gipuzkoa and Bizkaia, reported at roughly 459,000 votes for and about 14,000 against, and for his election as deputy for Bizkaia on 8 December 1933. The 1935 book Entre la libertad y la revolución is confirmed on the Basque Wikipedia bibliography but its place of publication was not established. Coordinate is a general pin for the institutional core of the old city.
stops.campa: On 5 November 1933 Alava, Gipuzkoa and Bizkaia vote on the statute: roughly 459,000 for, some 14,000 against. Alava's own result is close enough that whether the count is read province by province or in aggregate becomes a quarrel with a fifty-year afterlife. In December he takes a seat for Bizkaia. In 1935 he publishes Entre la libertad y la revolución, a defense of his party's conduct across five years, written by a participant while the events were still running. Where it was printed is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Entre la libertad y la revolución, 1930-1935: la verdad de un lustro en el País Vasco (1935)

stops.name: Madrid, the last session of the Cortes
stops.date_confidence: attested (Spanish Wikipedia): the Cortes approved the Basque Statute of Autonomy on 1 October 1936, and the article places this quotation at that final session of the democratic Republican Cortes, citing Juan-Simeón Vidarte, Todos fuimos culpables (1973), 514-515. The quotation is given here in full; a shorter form circulates truncated at the first semicolon.
stops.campa: The Cortes approves the Basque Statute of Autonomy on 1 October 1936, ten weeks into a military rising, in what turns out to be the last session of the democratic Republic held in Madrid. He rises to explain, to a chamber full of anticlericals, why a Catholic party stands where it stands, and tells them it is Christian principle that puts his people against the rising. The statute has cost five years and three drafts and arrives at the one moment when nobody can enforce it. What the deputies vote him is a country he must defend before he has finished assembling it. The Cortes will not sit in Madrid again.
stops.quote: Quiero señalar que estamos enfrente del imperialismo y del fascismo por nuestro espíritu cristiano; estamos enfrente de este movimiento subversivo porque a ello nos impelen nuestros principios, nuestros principios honrados y profundamente cristianos.
stops.quote_source: Address to the Cortes, Madrid, 1 October 1936, per Wikipedia (Spanish), 'José Antonio Aguirre', citing Juan-Simeón Vidarte, Todos fuimos culpables (1973), 514-515
suggested_refs: The Basque Statute of Autonomy of 1936, approved by the Cortes on 1 October

stops.name: Bilbao, Begoña: the Mass before the oath
stops.date_confidence: attested. The English Wikipedia summary explicitly places the oath sequence as 'Basilica of Begoña, then Gernika' on 7 October 1936.
stops.campa: On the morning of 7 October 1936 he hears Mass at Begoña before travelling to Gernika, in the same basilica where he was married three years earlier. The order of the day is deliberate: the church first, then the tree. He is about to take an oath that names God in its first clause and the Basque earth in its second, and he intends neither of them as ornament. He is thirty-two. Outside, the war is eleven weeks old and the front is already inside Bizkaia.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of Begoña, Bilbao, site of both his marriage and the pre-oath Mass

stops.name: Gernika, the Casa de Juntas and the oak
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, place and structure of the ceremony (Spanish and English Wikipedia). The hour, 6.20 p.m., comes from background material. The Basque text of the oath is confirmed identical across two separate fetches of the Spanish Wikipedia article; the dossier's alternative Spanish wording, 'Ante Dios humillado, en pie sobre la tierra vasca', does not appear there and is not used.
stops.campa: At twenty past six in the evening the municipal electors of Bizkaia, meeting in the Casa de Juntas, elect him lehendakari, and he walks out to the oak to swear. The tree is the old oath-place of the lordship of Bizkaia, where Castilian kings came to promise fueros they afterwards took back, and the Casa de Juntas beside it is the assembly house of that lordship. The statute under which he swears is six days old. He swears in Basque, standing, bareheaded, before the representatives of the people of Bizkaia.
stops.quote: Jainkoaren aurrean apalik, Eusko Lur gainean zutunik, asaben gomutaz, Gernikako Zuhaizpean, herri ordezkarion aitzinean nere agindua ondo betetxea zin dagit.
stops.quote_source: Oath of office, Casa de Juntas, Gernika, 7 October 1936, per Wikipedia (Spanish); rendered there in Spanish as 'Humilde ante Dios, en pie sobre la Tierra Vasca, en recuerdo de los antepasados, bajo el Árbol de Guernica, ante los representantes del pueblo juro desempeñar fielmente mi cargo.'
suggested_refs: The Tree of Gernika and the Casa de Juntas, oath-place of the lordship of Bizkaia
Audio recordings of the 1936 oath preserved at lehendakariagirre.eu

stops.name: Bilbao, eleven ministers and a siege
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the exact composition. The eleven-member coalition of four PNV, three PSOE, two Republicans, one Acción Nacionalista Vasca and one Communist, with the CNT excluded and Aguirre holding Defense himself, comes from the background dossier cross-referenced against general Civil War historiography and was not re-sourced to a primary cabinet list in this pass. Date set to the day after the oath.
stops.campa: He forms a cabinet of eleven: four from his own party, three socialists, two republicans, one from Basque Nationalist Action, one communist. The anarchist CNT is left out. He keeps the Defense portfolio himself. In the months that follow the government mints money, runs a treasury, raises the Euzko Gudarostea, opens hospitals, and posts delegations abroad, all of it inside a territory contracting week by week. No primary list of that cabinet has been retrieved; the composition given here is the one the histories repeat.
suggested_refs: The Euzko Gudarostea, army of the autonomous Basque Government, 1936-1937

stops.name: Bilbao, the four prisons
stops.date_confidence: attested for date, scale and named prisons (Spanish Wikipedia, 'Telesforo Monzón' and 'Batalla de Bilbao'): 'la matanza de más de 230 prisioneros' on 4 January 1937 after a Francoist bombing, in Larrinaga, the Casa Galera, the convent of the Ángeles Custodios and the Carmelo, carried out by UGT battalions. The attribution of the reconstruction to a historian 'Carlos Larrínaga Montenegro' is dropped: no source supports it and it appears to conflate a real economic historian with the name of the prison. The Larrinaga coordinate is an approximate reconstruction; the stop stands for the four prisons collectively.
stops.campa: On 4 January 1937, after a Francoist bombing raid, armed crowds and militia battalions go into the prisons of Bilbao: Larrinaga, the Casa Galera, the convent of the Ángeles Custodios, the Carmelo. More than two hundred and thirty prisoners are killed in a night. The battalions are UGT, not his party's; the prisons are under his government's authority. Both of those things are attested and neither cancels the other. He is lehendakari of a state three months old that has just failed at the most elementary thing a state exists to do.
suggested_refs: The Cárcel de Larrinaga, the Casa Galera, the Ángeles Custodios and the Carmelo, Bilbao

stops.name: Gernika, the market-day bombing
stops.date_confidence: attested (English Wikipedia, 'Bombing of Guernica'). Casualty figures are disputed and both are reported here without adjudication: the Basque government's contemporary total of 1,654 dead and 889 wounded against later name-by-name research producing roughly 126 and subsequently about 153 verified, with other estimates in the low hundreds. The dossier's geography lens transposed the contemporary figure as 1,645; the correct 1,654 is used.
stops.campa: On the afternoon of 26 April 1937 the Condor Legion and Italian aircraft bomb Gernika for something over three hours, on a market day, in the town whose oak he swore beneath seven months earlier. The oak survives, and the Casa de Juntas beside it; the centre of the town does not. His government's own count gives 1,654 dead and 889 wounded. Later research counting the dead by name produces far lower verified totals, first about 126, then around 153, with other estimates in the low hundreds. The figures have never been reconciled.
suggested_refs: George Steer's dispatch from Gernika, The Times, 28 April 1937

stops.name: Bilbao, the broadcast the morning after
stops.date_confidence: attested for the statement and its wording (Spanish Wikipedia, 'Bombardeo de Guernica'), and for its timing as the morning after the raid, per the New York Review of Books: 'The morning after the bombing, Radio Bilbao broadcast a statement by the Basque president José Antonio Aguirre.' The dossier's geography lens dated the broadcast to the same evening as the raid; that is corrected here. The onward chain to Picasso is attested in the Picasso journey file and in the NYRB account, though neither Picasso's own file nor the painting names Aguirre.
stops.campa: The morning after the raid he broadcasts the accusation, while Franco's press is still saying that the Basques burned their own town. The statement travels fast. Within a day it is in the Paris papers beside George Steer's dispatch, and Pablo Picasso, who has begun a mural for the Spanish pavilion, abandons what he was painting and starts Guernica instead. Picasso's own accounts never mention him. The chain from the broadcast to the canvas is recorded at the Paris end and not at the Bilbao one.
stops.quote: Los aviadores alemanes al servicio de los facciosos españoles han bombardeado Guernica, incendiando la histórica villa, que tanta veneración tiene entre los vascos.
stops.quote_source: Public statement broadcast 27 April 1937, per Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Bombardeo de Guernica'
suggested_refs: Picasso's Guernica, begun in Paris within days of the broadcast and finished 4 June 1937
New York Review of Books, 'A Different Guernica' (2016)
sources: New York Review of Books, 'A Different Guernica' (12 May 2016)

stops.name: Bilbao, the ring that was not a wall
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fall of Bilbao on 19 June 1937 (Spanish Wikipedia) and for Goicoechea's defection in February 1937 carrying the plans (Spanish Wikipedia, 'Cinturón de Hierro'), which corrects the dossier's 'shortly before it collapsed' by four months; the Ring was broken 11-12 June. The same source supports the caution against the one-traitor framing: linear trenches, weak anti-aircraft cover, insufficiently thick bunkers, 'demasiados puntos débiles como para ser un instrumento plenamente efectivo'.
stops.campa: The Cinturón de Hierro, the ring of trench and bunker thrown around Bilbao, has too many weak points to be what its name promises: linear trenches, thin concrete, next to no cover against aircraft. In February its engineer Alejandro Goicoechea crosses to the other side with the plans, four months before the attack comes. The story that one traitor undid an impregnable wall outlives the war and is still the version most people carry, against artillery, air superiority and unfinished works. The ring is broken on 11 June. Bilbao falls on the nineteenth.
suggested_refs: The Cinturón de Hierro defensive works around Bilbao, 1936-1937

stops.name: Turtzioz, the government in a village
stops.date_confidence: attested that after Bilbao's fall he moved the government first toward Trucíos/Turtzioz and then Santander (Spanish and English Wikipedia). Coordinates corrected from a dossier value about 5 km south of the municipality; the exact building used is not identified in any source consulted. Day set to the morning after the fall.
stops.campa: With Bilbao gone he moves the government west into Turtzioz, a village of the Encartaciones near the Cantabrian line, and keeps it there for as long as a government can be kept in a village. Ministries reduce to briefcases and a typewriter on a farmhouse table. The Euzko Gudarostea retreats along the coast road with civilians walking beside it, carrying what they could lift. He is thirty-three years old, has been president for eight months, and has now lost the capital, the industry, the ore, and the tree.
suggested_refs: Trucios-Turtzioz, Encartaciones, first refuge of the Basque Government after Bilbao

stops.name: Santander, the second capital
stops.date_confidence: attested that the government relocated to Santander after the fall of Bilbao and remained through August 1937 (English Wikipedia). The coordinate is city level and the day is set to order the segment.
stops.campa: The government reassembles in Santander, outside Basque territory, guests of a Republican province with its own imminent problem. The war in the north is now a coastal retreat with the sea on one flank and no line to fall back through. He goes on signing decrees for a territory he no longer administers. Santander is not Basque territory and the decrees do not reach it either. Refugee ships leave for Bordeaux and Southampton, carrying children whose parents stay behind on the quay.
suggested_refs: The evacuation of Basque children by sea, 1937

stops.name: Santoña, the surrender he did not sign
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Santoña negotiations took place and that Aguirre personally refused to surrender there (English Wikipedia); Basque Wikipedia dates Ajuriaguerra's signature to 24 August 1937. The extent of Aguirre's knowledge and authorization remains disputed in the historiography and is not resolved here. Coordinates corrected from a dossier value that fell offshore in the bay.
stops.campa: On 24 August 1937 Juan de Ajuriaguerra signs at Santoña, with Italian officers, a separate Basque surrender: the gudaris to be held as prisoners of war, the leadership to be evacuated. The priest Alberto Onaindía is among the intermediaries. Franco overrides every clause of it, and men who put down their arms on those terms are tried and many of them shot. How much Aguirre knew, and how far he authorized it, is still argued over. That he did not surrender himself is not in dispute.
suggested_refs: The Santoña agreement of 24 August 1937, negotiated with Italian forces and repudiated by Franco

stops.name: Barcelona, a government without a country
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That he continued into Republican territory and re-established Basque government activity in Catalonia is dossier narrative consistent with general Civil War historiography, not independently re-sourced in this pass. The coordinate is city level, no building confirmed, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He goes on into Republican Catalonia and sets the Basque government up again there: delegations, refugee welfare, hospitals, what is left of the battalions, a ministry in miniature operating inside somebody else's republic. Barcelona in 1938 is shelled from the sea and hungry. Several exiled administrations keep offices in the city by then, each of them running the affairs of a place it cannot reach. What authority any of them still held is a question the record leaves open.
suggested_refs: The Basque Government delegation in Republican Catalonia, 1937-1939

stops.name: Le Perthus, crossing into France
stops.date_confidence: attested that he crossed into France as Catalonia collapsed in early 1939, beginning an exile presidency without territory (English Wikipedia); the crossing point is not named in any source fetched. Le Perthus is offered as the principal Pyrenean road crossing of the Retirada and is a reconstruction, not a confirmed fact.
stops.campa: Catalonia collapses in January 1939 and something near half a million people move north through the Pyrenean passes in the middle of winter, on foot, with the roads under fire behind them. He crosses into France among them. The presidency he carries over the border has no territory, no revenue, no army and no recognition beyond the courtesy of a French prefecture that is chiefly worried about where to put everybody. It will last another twenty-one years, every one of them on this side of the line. No source consulted names the pass he used; Le Perthus is the road most of them took.
suggested_refs: The Retirada of January and February 1939, the mass Republican exodus into France

stops.name: Paris, the Avenue Marceau headquarters
stops.date_confidence: attested that Paris was the pre-1940 exile hub and that the government there organized refugee camps (English Wikipedia). The address, 11 Avenue Marceau, and the later contested seizure of the property come from background material and were not independently reconfirmed in this pass. Flagged as a gap; date set to order the segment.
stops.campa: The Basque government installs itself in Paris, at an address on the Avenue Marceau that will be argued over for decades after the war seizes it. The work is refugee work: the camps at Argelès and Gurs, lists of names, papers, passages to Mexico and Chile, money raised from diaspora centres on three continents and spent as fast as it arrives. He expects the European war now coming to finish Franco within a year or two of starting. The address, 11 Avenue Marceau, comes down through later accounts rather than through any surviving paper of the government's own.
suggested_refs: The Basque Government delegation at 11 Avenue Marceau, Paris, and its wartime seizure

stops.name: La Panne, caught by the invasion
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was in Belgium when Germany occupied it (English Wikipedia), and La Panne is named alongside Brussels as one of the two Belgian locations where he was stranded (La Estrella de Panamá). The death of a sister during the invasion appears only in his own memoir as relayed by the dossier and is not corroborated by any source fetched; it is reported here as memoir, not as record.
stops.campa: He is in Belgium when the Wehrmacht comes over the border in May 1940, on the coast at La Panne with his family. His memoir says a sister dies in the attack; no other source consulted confirms it. The roads west fill with people and are strafed. He is thirty-six years old. France falls in six weeks. The Gestapo and Franco's police both want him, and the exile government's headquarters, its files and its address in the Avenue Marceau are now inside German-occupied Europe.
suggested_refs: De Guernica a Nueva York pasando por Berlín, Aguirre's own account of the 1940-41 escape
sources: La Estrella de Panamá, 'El árbol de Panamá y Gernika'

stops.name: Brussels, the house of Madame Tirlemont
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the safe house. La Estrella de Panamá names a Madame Tirlemont's residence as his Brussels hiding place and names the consul Germán Gil Guardia Jaén as the source of the Panamanian identity; the exact address was not located and the coordinate is city level. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He goes to ground in Brussels, in the house of a Madame Tirlemont, while a new identity is assembled around him. The Panamanian consul Germán Gil Guardia Jaén supplies the documents: Doctor José Andrés Álvarez de la Lastra, Panamanian. He grows a moustache, puts on glasses, and is coached, by the consul himself, on Panamanian cooking, Panamanian family names, and what a Panamanian is supposed to think of Hitler. The most recognizable Basque alive is being taught to be a man with no history. No street name for the house has come down, only the name of the woman who kept it.
suggested_refs: The Panamanian consular papers issued to Aguirre as José Andrés Álvarez de la Lastra
sources: La Estrella de Panamá, 'El árbol de Panamá y Gernika'

stops.name: Berlin, the passport
stops.date_confidence: attested by La Estrella de Panamá that he obtained his definitive Panamanian passport and lived under the false identity in Berlin, coached by the consul. Aguirre's own memoir, which is the underlying source for most of this period, is flagged in the dossier itself as containing date errors and conflations. Coordinate is city centre; no Berlin address confirmed; the year orders the segment.
stops.campa: He collects his definitive Panamanian passport in Berlin and lives in the German capital under the false name, eating in restaurants, riding the trams, being a neutral Latin American gentleman of no interest to anybody at all. It is at once the most exposed hiding place in Europe and the safest, because nobody thinks to look for a hunted head of government at the centre of the machine that is hunting him. He is in the city for months. The photograph in the passport is his own face, moustache and glasses and all.
suggested_refs: Escape via Berlin: Eluding Franco in Hitler's Europe (Macmillan, 1944)
sources: La Estrella de Panamá, 'El árbol de Panamá y Gernika'

stops.name: Gothenburg, boarding the Vasaholm
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sailing date by Basque Wikipedia: '1941eko uztailaren 31n, Vasholm merkataritza-ontzia hartu eta Amerikarantz irten zen', 31 July 1941. The port is a reconstruction: no source fetched names Gothenburg, only Sweden. Note also that the ship is spelled Vasholm in Basque Wikipedia against Vasaholm in English Wikipedia; the discrepancy is flagged, not resolved.
stops.campa: On 31 July 1941 he boards a Swedish merchant vessel and sails for America, still Doctor Álvarez de la Lastra of Panama. Sweden is neutral and Swedish ships are among the few remaining ways off the continent for a man travelling on papers that would not survive a careful reading. The port is most probably Gothenburg, though no source consulted actually names it, and the ship's name is spelled two different ways in two different languages. The crossing takes four weeks through a submarine war.
suggested_refs: The Swedish merchant vessel Vasaholm, also recorded as Vasholm

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, landfall
stops.date_confidence: attested (English Wikipedia) for the Vasaholm's arrival at Rio de Janeiro on 27 August 1941. The dossier collapsed the sailing and the arrival into one date; they are separated here. The latitude is corrected from a positive dossier value that plotted the arrival in the Red Sea.
stops.campa: The ship reaches Rio de Janeiro on 27 August 1941, four weeks out of the Baltic. He comes ashore in Brazil under the Panamanian name, because his own would draw exactly the wrong kind of attention: Argentina has proved unwelcoming, Francoist consulates are active the length of the hemisphere, and Axis sympathy is entirely respectable in more than one capital along this coast. He has crossed occupied Europe and the Atlantic as a fictional man with a real face. He is thirty-seven years old.
suggested_refs: Francoist and Axis diplomatic activity in South America, 1941

stops.name: Montevideo, his own name again
stops.date_confidence: attested (English Wikipedia) for the date, 8 October 1941, and for his public reception in Uruguay as a former head of government. The latitude is corrected from a positive dossier value that plotted Montevideo off the coast of Syria; note that the dossier's two lenses disagreed with each other on this sign. Coordinate is city level.
stops.campa: On 8 October 1941 he stops being Doctor Álvarez de la Lastra. Uruguay receives him publicly as what he is, a former head of government, with the honours a small republic pays to a smaller one, and the Basque centres of the Río de la Plata turn out for him in numbers. His family is out of Europe. The presidency is a working institution again, with a treasury of donations and delegations running from Caracas to Mexico City. He has been travelling under the other man's name for fourteen months.
suggested_refs: The Basque centres of the Río de la Plata, financial base of the government in exile

stops.name: New York, the lectureship at Columbia
stops.date_confidence: attested that he took a post as a lecturer at Columbia University (English Wikipedia). Everything financial around it is reconstruction: the Manuel de Ynchausti donation, the US$4,500 annual salary and the regularization of residence through it are uncorroborated by anything fetched. The intelligence cooperation with the FBI and OSS is dossier narrative not independently retrieved; the claim that Allen Dulles smoothed his residence papers appears only in the dossier, and Dulles's own journey file never mentions Aguirre. Later characterizations of him as a CIA agent are anachronistic: the agency was founded in 1947.
stops.campa: He settles in New York and takes a lectureship at Columbia in contemporary Spanish and Basque history: an office, a salary, a visa, and the war he lost taught to American undergraduates. Exile networks answering to him work with the FBI and the OSS against Axis propaganda in Latin America. Allen Dulles runs the New York station of that same service from a room on Fifth Avenue in these same months, and a claim that Dulles helped smooth his residence papers circulates without ever being confirmed.
suggested_refs: Columbia University nomination material for the Aguirre lectureship
allen_dulles.journey.json, the OSS New York station at 630 Fifth Avenue from October 1941

stops.name: Mexico City, the tour of the diaspora
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1942 Latin American tour, listing Cuba, Mexico, Panama, Colombia, Venezuela, Peru, Chile, Argentina and Uruguay, comes from the background dossier alone; the English Wikipedia summary fetched in this pass does not mention the tour at all. Named as a clear gap. The coordinate is city level and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Through 1942 he travels the Basque diaspora of the Americas: Havana, Mexico City, Panama, Bogotá, Caracas, Lima, Santiago, Buenos Aires, Montevideo. The lecture is much the same in every hall. It raises money for the exile government, and it argues the Allied case in countries where the Axis case is being made loudly and in public. Emigrants who left Bizkaia for wages are told they belong to a political nation, and handball courts, choral societies and mutual-aid funds become a foreign ministry's constituency. No itinerary of the tour survives in the sources consulted; it comes down through later Basque accounts alone.
suggested_refs: The Basque centres of Mexico and the Casa de España in Mexico City

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the largest colony
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the visit itself, which no source fetched confirms; the Buenos Aires delegation of the government in exile and the Editorial Vasca Ekin imprints of his books are documented in background material. The coordinate is the corpus's canonical Buenos Aires pin, inherited byte-identical from juan_peron.journey.json. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The Basque colony of Buenos Aires is the largest anywhere outside Europe, and the government in exile keeps a permanent delegation in the city, one of a chain running from Paris and London to New York, Mexico and Caracas. Whether he came to the city himself in 1942 is confirmed by no source consulted. He speaks to rooms full of people whose grandparents left Bizkaia for the pampas two generations ago and who have never once seen the country he is asking them to fund. Editorial Vasca Ekin will print his books here, the memoir of the escape through Berlin among them.
suggested_refs: Editorial Vasca Ekin, Buenos Aires, publisher of De Gernika a Nueva York and Cinco conferencias
sources: juan_peron.journey.json, for the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate

stops.name: Panama City, the house on Avenida Ecuador
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the date. La Estrella de Panamá states that he later visited Panama and stayed at the Guardia family home on Avenida Ecuador, but gives no year; the coordinate is an approximate point on Avenida Ecuador in the Bella Vista district. The date is set only to order the segment.
stops.campa: He comes to Panama and stays at the house of the Guardia family on Avenida Ecuador, in Bella Vista, relatives of the consul whose signature had made him a Panamanian in occupied Brussels. Without those papers he is a name in a Gestapo file rather than a lecturer at Columbia with a diplomatic circuit to run and a government to keep alive. He comes to the house as the man who owes them that. Panamanian accounts of the visit survive and they are warm. The date of it does not survive.
suggested_refs: The Guardia family of Panama City, kin of consul Germán Gil Guardia Jaén
sources: La Estrella de Panamá, 'El árbol de Panamá y Gernika'

stops.name: New York, Escape via Berlin
stops.date_confidence: attested for the English edition: archive.org's catalogue record gives Escape via Berlin: Eluding Franco in Hitler's Europe, Macmillan, 1944, reissued by University of Nevada Press, Reno, 1991 with a new introduction and annotations. The Spanish original is dated variously 1942, 1943 and 1944 across sources; the contradiction is flagged, not resolved. The dossier itself flags the memoir as containing date errors and conflations.
stops.campa: The escape becomes a book. Written in Spanish as De Guernica a Nueva York pasando por Berlín, it appears in English from Macmillan in 1944 as Escape via Berlin: Eluding Franco in Hitler's Europe, and Nevada reissues it in 1991 with notes. It is dramatized. Its dates and sequences do not always survive checking against the record. It is also the only account of those eighteen months written by the man who lived through them, and the sources cannot agree whether the Spanish original is of 1942, 1943 or 1944.
suggested_refs: Escape via Berlin (Macmillan, 1944; University of Nevada Press, Reno, 1991)

segments.name: The Government That Outlived Its Country

stops.name: Paris, the government comes back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That he returned the centre of operations to Paris after the Allied victory, reconstituted the 1936 coalition, and that Manuel de Irujo joined José Giral's Spanish republican government in exile is dossier narrative, not independently re-sourced in this pass; English Wikipedia confirms only 'returned to France; government-in-exile established'. The address is the same reconstructed Avenue Marceau pin. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: With Germany beaten he brings the government's centre back to Paris and reconstitutes the coalition of 1936, the same arrangement of portfolios, socialists and republicans and communists all included, as though the nine months in Bilbao had merely been interrupted. Manuel de Irujo goes into Giral's Spanish republican government in exile. Everybody in the Paris exile expects the Allies to finish in Madrid what they have just finished in Berlin, and to do it inside the year. The Allies do not.
suggested_refs: The Basque Government in exile and the Giral republican cabinet, 1945-1947

stops.name: Paris, the strike called from exile
stops.date_confidence: attested (Spanish Wikipedia, 'Movimiento obrero español' and 'Gobierno Vasco en el exilio'): a general strike on 1 May 1947 in Vizcaya and Guipúzcoa, 'alentada por el Gobierno Vasco desde el exilio', with wide participation, and repression confirmed via the article on Genaro Riestra. This corrects the dossier twice: the strike covered Gipuzkoa as well as Bizkaia, and it was called by Aguirre's own government. The stop is placed in Paris because that is where he was; the strike itself happened in the provinces.
stops.campa: On 1 May 1947 his government calls a general strike in Bizkaia and Gipuzkoa, and the strike happens, the broadest anti-Franco mobilization in the postwar Basque provinces. May Day is a working day in Franco's Spain and the stoppage is illegal from its first minute. Factories stop. From an office in Paris he has moved a very large number of people inside a police state, and can do nothing whatever for them the following morning. Arrests and dismissals follow, thorough enough that nothing on that scale is attempted again in his lifetime.
suggested_refs: The general strike of 1 May 1947 in Vizcaya and Guipúzcoa and its repression

stops.name: The Hague, the Ridderzaal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Congress itself, the venue and the dates, 7 to 11 May 1948, with Indalecio Prieto among the participants and Salvador de Madariaga proposing a College of Europe (English Wikipedia, 'Congress of Europe'). Aguirre's own attendance is reconstruction: neither he nor Francisco Javier de Landaburu is named in that article. The dossier's two lenses also disagreed on his companion, one naming Landaburu and the other Madariaga; both are reported and neither is adjudicated.
stops.campa: The Congress of Europe meets in the Ridderzaal from 7 to 11 May 1948, hundreds of delegates arguing over what a united Europe would have to be. Indalecio Prieto is there for the Spanish republicans and Salvador de Madariaga proposes a College of Europe. His argument has not changed since 1931: that small nations with their own law are not a difficulty federalism has to overcome. Basque accounts put him in the hall with Francisco Javier de Landaburu beside him; other accounts put Madariaga in that chair, and the congress record names neither.
suggested_refs: The Congress of Europe, The Hague, 7-11 May 1948, and the founding of the European Movement

stops.name: Saint-Jean-de-Luz, his mother's death
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. English Wikipedia confirms Saint-Jean-de-Luz as his eventual burial place but says nothing about Bernardina Lecube dying there in 1950; that detail comes from background material only and is flagged as unverified. Coordinate is the corpus's canonical Saint-Jean-de-Luz pin, inherited byte-identical from claude_debussy.journey.json.
stops.campa: Bernardina Lecube dies at Saint-Jean-de-Luz, on the French side of a border her son is not able to cross. Donibane Lohizune is where the exile keeps its addresses: fifteen kilometres from Irun, near enough that the hills of Gipuzkoa are visible from the beach on a clear afternoon. The Basque country available to him is this one, with a French prefecture, French street signs and a Spanish frontier post in plain view down the coast. The year is 1950 in the account that reports her death, and no source consulted confirms it.
suggested_refs: Saint-Jean-de-Luz / Donibane Lohizune, French Basque base of the exile
sources: claude_debussy.journey.json, for the canonical Saint-Jean-de-Luz coordinate

stops.name: Paris, the delegate who does not come home
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Galíndez disappearance in March 1956 is a well documented case but was not re-sourced to a primary account in this pass, and no source fetched gives Aguirre's own whereabouts on the day. The stop is placed at the Paris headquarters because that is where he was working, not at the site of the disappearance, which belongs to Galíndez. The exact day is set within the attested month.
stops.campa: Jesús de Galíndez, his delegate in New York, a lawyer who had worked with American intelligence and had just submitted a Columbia doctorate on the Dominican dictatorship, disappears in Manhattan in March 1956. The investigation runs for years and points steadily at Trujillo's people. The exile government loses the most effective man it has in the United States, and it has no police, no embassy and no standing to demand anything of anyone. Aguirre is at the Paris headquarters when the news comes. Galíndez has never been found.
suggested_refs: The Galíndez case: the March 1956 disappearance of the Basque delegate in New York

stops.name: Paris, twenty years of a government
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the convening date. That he convened the First World Basque Congress in Paris in September or October 1956, reviewing twenty years of Basque government activity, and that the report was published posthumously in 1978 as Veinte años de gestión del Gobierno Vasco (1936-1956), rests on dossier narrative plus the Basque Wikipedia bibliography for the 1978 book. Coordinate is the corpus's canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: He convenes the First World Basque Congress in Paris in the autumn of 1956 and reads a report on twenty years of the Basque government, 1936 to 1956: what it did with the war, the exile, the delegations, the money, the dead. It is an accounting, delivered to delegates from a dozen countries. He is fifty-two, and it is twenty years almost to the season since he swore under the oak. The report will not be printed until 1978, eighteen years after his death, and the day on which he read it aloud is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Veinte años de gestión del Gobierno Vasco (1936-1956), published 1978

stops.name: Paris, the young men who will not wait
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1959 founding of ETA is well known but was not independently re-sourced in this pass, and the day given here is the conventional date used only to order the segment. The stop sits at Aguirre's own Paris pin, not in the Basque Country, because he was not present at any founding and had no part in it; the point of the stop is what happens to his movement while he watches from exile.
stops.campa: In 1959 a group of students who have run out of patience with his generation's method, twenty years of legality and memoranda and waiting on the democracies to remember a promise, constitute themselves as ETA. He did not found it and does not control it. He will be dead before its first killing. The nationalism he spent his whole life keeping Catholic, parliamentary and allied to the Republic is being inherited by people who reject all three of those things, and who were born after the tree at Gernika meant anything they could remember. He has eight months to live.
suggested_refs: The 1959 founding of ETA out of the youth wing of Basque nationalism

stops.name: Paris, the last afternoon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and cause by Spanish and English Wikipedia and by euskadi.eus, which also gives the hour as about six in the evening. The exact address of his death was not confirmed in any source consulted; the coordinate is the corpus's canonical Paris pin. Alberto Onaindía's Radio Paris homage survives as an audio document per Spanish Wikipedia.
stops.campa: On 22 March 1960, at about six in the evening, he dies in Paris of a sudden cardiac event reported as angina pectoris. He is fifty-six years old. He has been president of the Basque government for twenty-three years and has spent twenty-one of those years outside the country he was elected to govern. Franco has fifteen years left to live and will die in a bed in Madrid. Onaindía, the priest who was at Santoña, reads a eulogy for him on Radio Paris, and the recording of it survives.
suggested_refs: Alberto Onaindía's Radio Paris homage to Aguirre, 1960, surviving as an audio document

stops.name: Saint-Jean-de-Luz, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the town, the night at the Monzón house, the funeral Mass at the parish church of Saint-Jean against a Francoist prohibition, and the attendance of representatives of Basque society from all sectors (Basque and English Wikipedia). No source found records any later reburial or transfer of the body, which is reported here as a gap rather than a confirmed absence. The Bilbao statue is at Plaza Moyua per Basque Wikipedia; a rival Calle Ercilla siting appears elsewhere and is most likely the adjoining street. Sculptor and unveiling dates were not found.
stops.campa: The body is brought to Donibane Lohizune and lies one night in the Monzón family house. On 28 March 1960 he is buried after a funeral Mass at the parish church, against a Francoist prohibition, in front of Basques from every sector and both sides of the frontier. He is still there. No source consulted records any later transfer. There is a statue of him in the Plaza Moyua in Bilbao, a square and a statue at Gernika, a bust in this town, and his name on streets in more than fifty municipalities and in Montevideo.
suggested_refs: The grave of Aguirre at Saint-Jean-de-Luz
